opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to understand it is that in China, open models have become a kind of strategic default rather than a charitable choice. If you're a company like Meituan or Xiaomi, you have enormous product surfaces: delivery logistics, local services, phones, cars, smart home devices. AI is going to touch all of those, and you don't want to be dependent on someone else's API for something that core to your business. So step one is just building the in-house capability. Once you have it, the question becomes: why open it up?

And there are a few good answers. One is talent. The best researchers want their work to be seen, cited, and used. If you're a company that people historically think of as a food delivery platform or a phone maker, releasing a strong open-weight model is the fastest way to signal to the research community that you're a serious AI lab. It's recruiting through artifacts. The second is ecosystem and mindshare. In China especially, after DeepSeek and Qwen showed that open releases can make you the reference point for an entire developer community, there's real pressure to participate. If you stay closed, you're kind of invisible in that conversation.

The third thing is that the economics of releasing weights are different than people assume. For most of these companies, the model itself isn't the product they're selling. Meituan isn't trying to win the API market; they're trying to make their services better. So giving away the weights costs them relatively little competitively, and they get feedback, fine-tunes, bug reports, and goodwill in return. It's somewhat like what Meta was doing with Llama early on: commoditize the layer that isn't your core moat.

And then there's a national and cultural dimension. There's a sense among Chinese labs that open releases are how they compete globally, especially with constraints on compute. If you can't necessarily outspend the frontier American labs, you can out-distribute them. Open models get adopted everywhere, in startups, in academia, in other countries, and that creates influence that's hard to get with a closed API.

So for me, Meituan and Xiaomi doing this is a sign of how normalized it's become. It's no longer just the pure AI labs. Big consumer tech companies see releasing open models as part of what it means to be a credible technology company in China right now. And honestly, for the open ecosystem as a whole, more serious players training and releasing models is a great thing. It means more diversity of approaches and more data points about what actually works.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will touch the companies’ product areas, but does not attribute to Meituan and Xiaomi an expectation that users will widely use AI agents.

r002.rationale: It gives no example of a Meituan agent helping users decide what request to make.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to understand it is that these companies have looked at the landscape and concluded that the model is not the product for them. Meituan is a delivery and local services business. Xiaomi sells phones, cars, and a whole ecosystem of devices. Neither of them is trying to win by charging people per token for API access. So the question they're asking isn't "how do we beat OpenAI," it's "how do we make sure we have the capability in-house and aren't dependent on someone else's roadmap and someone else's pricing."

Once you frame it that way, open-sourcing becomes pretty rational rather than altruistic. If you're not going to monetize the weights directly, releasing them costs you very little commercially, and it buys you a lot. You get recruiting, because the strongest researchers want to work on things that get seen and cited. You get credibility, because the market now treats shipping a competitive open model as proof that you're a serious technology company and not just an app layer. And you get a feedback loop with the community, where people fine-tune your model, find its failures, and build tooling around it that you'd otherwise have to build yourself. DeepSeek really changed the calculus here. It showed a Chinese lab could get global attention with a release, and that attention is worth something to a brand like Xiaomi.

There's also a strategic layer specific to China. Access to the frontier closed models from the US is uncertain, and compute is constrained. If you're a company that is going to deploy models into hundreds of millions of devices or into a logistics operation, you want to control the stack. Owning the training recipe matters more than owning any single checkpoint, because the checkpoint goes stale in six months but the team and the data pipeline don't. Meituan releasing something like LongCat is partly a signal that they've built that pipeline.

And honestly, part of it is just how the ecosystem in China works. Open weights have become the default competitive move. Alibaba did it with Qwen and got enormous adoption. Once Qwen is everywhere, a company like Xiaomi has to decide whether to build on Alibaba's model forever or have its own. Having your own gives you optionality, even if internally you end up using a mix. So I read it less as "everyone wants to be a foundation model lab" and more as "being able to train a good model has become table stakes for a large Chinese tech company, and open-sourcing is the cheapest way to prove you can."

The thing I'd watch is whether they sustain it. Releasing one strong model is a talent and compute story. Releasing a second and third, keeping up with the frontier, is a much harder commitment, and I think we'll see some of these efforts quietly fade while the ones tied to a real product need, like on-device models for Xiaomi's hardware, persist.

r001.rationale: The response discusses in-house model capability and product strategy, but does not say Meituan and Xiaomi expect AI agents to become widely used by users.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe a Meituan agent helping users decide what request to make.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it less as, “Why does every company want to compete with the leading AI lab?” and more as, “How important could this technology become to their core business?” If you think models are going to be a fundamental part of your products, there’s a strong incentive to build the expertise internally.

For Meituan, you can imagine applications across a service platform—helping customers find what they want, giving merchants better tools, or automating internal work. For Xiaomi, the connection is devices: how do you build an assistant that works well across your products? Owning more of the model development gives you control over cost, latency, and how closely the model fits those experiences.

Then open source is a separate strategic choice. It can help you attract researchers and developers, get feedback, and establish yourself as a serious participant in AI. You don’t necessarily need to make money by selling access to the model if it makes your existing business more valuable.

I wouldn’t claim to know their internal reasoning, but that’s the framework I’d use: they have businesses that could benefit from AI, and developing models builds both a useful capability today and more options for the future.

r001.rationale: The response says AI models could become fundamental to products, but does not attribute to Meituan and Xiaomi an expectation that AI agents will become widely used by users.

r002.rationale: It mentions helping Meituan customers find what they want, but does not describe an agent helping users decide what request to make.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to understand it is that these companies don’t need to become an AI lab in the same sense as OpenAI. They already have large businesses, distribution, and very specific places where better models could create value.

For Meituan, you can imagine applications around local services, helping users decide what to buy, and tools for merchants. For Xiaomi, there’s an obvious connection to phones, devices, and the software experience across them. Having their own models gives them more control over cost, latency, and how those experiences evolve, instead of depending entirely on another company’s API.

And open source can serve a different purpose from the product itself. You release a strong model, people start experimenting with it, developers become familiar with your work, and it helps you recruit researchers. You can share the underlying model while still building a differentiated business around your products and customers.

I wouldn’t assume there’s one single motivation, or that we know their internal strategy. But strategically, it makes sense: if AI is going to become an important layer of your existing business, you want the expertise to build it and the option to control it yourself.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may become an important layer of existing businesses, but does not attribute an expectation that AI agents will become widely used by users.

r002.rationale: It mentions helping Meituan users decide what to buy, but does not describe an agent helping them determine what request to make.
